summary: Describes TCP Cookie Transactions, an experimental TCP extension meant to resist connection spoofing and resource exhaustion by letting a server avoid keeping state during the initial handshake. The cookie exchange can carry limited data. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7805.

eli5.summary: A server usually must remember everyone who knocks, even fakers. This idea made the knocker carry a token so the server did not need to remember. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 7805.

subtitle: A TCP extension that uses cryptographic cookies to defeat SYN floods and let servers avoid keeping connection state during the handshake.

tldr.problem: TCP servers are vulnerable to SYN flood attacks where attackers send thousands of forged connection requests. Servers must keep state for each incoming connection request, wasting memory and CPU. Even legitimate servers need to track connection state during the three-way handshake before knowing if the client is real.
tldr.mechanism: Both the client and server exchange cryptographic cookies during the TCP handshake. The server only creates connection state after verifying the client's cookie, allowing the server to remain stateless during the initial exchange. The cookie pair protects against spoofing and replay attacks.
tldr.outcome: The specification is experimental and has been superseded by RFC 7805. The cookie approach was adopted in later protocols like DCCP and influenced SYN cookie designs.

today: RFC 6013 is an Experimental protocol that has been superseded by RFC 7805. While TCPCT itself was not widely deployed, the cookie concept influenced later designs. SYN cookies (embedded in the initial sequence number) became more common, and the approach was adopted in protocols like SCTP and DCCP.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
The TCP three-way handshake normally requires servers to allocate a connection control block (TCB) immediately when a SYN is received. In a SYN flood attack, an attacker sends many SYN packets with forged source addresses. The server allocates state for each one, consuming memory and CPU. Once the attack traffic stops, the server is left with thousands of half-open connections that time out.

TCP Cookie Transactions (TCPCT) eliminate server state during the initial handshake. Both parties exchange cookies: cryptographically unpredictable values that serve as authentication tokens. The server only allocates connection state after receiving a valid cookie pair in the third packet, making the server stateless and therefore immune to SYN flooding.
sections.eli5: Instead of remembering every person who rings the doorbell, the server gives them a sealed token to carry. When they come back with the token, the server knows they are real and can let them in.

sections.title: How the Cookie Exchange Works
sections.content:
The exchange happens in three phases. In the first phase, the client sends a SYN packet containing a cookie and optionally some application data. The server responds with a SYN-ACK containing its own cookie and optionally response data. The server does not allocate any state at this point.

In the second phase, the client sends an ACK with both the client and server cookies and retransmits its SYN options. The server verifies the server cookie by regenerating it from the incoming packet and comparing it to what the client echoed back. Once verified, the server allocates connection state.

The exchange relies on TCP Timestamps and the cookie pair to protect against insertion and reflection attacks. Timestamps indicate when each party sent its message, and the cookie pair is verified by both sides before creating state.
sections.eli5: The client shows its badge to the server. The server gives the client a token. The client comes back with both the badge and the token. The server checks that the token is correct and the badge matches. Only then does the server create a record of the conversation.

sections.title: Generating Cookies
sections.content:
Cookies must be unpredictable and must depend on the client's address and port, the server's port, and any data the client sends. A recommended method is to use a cryptographic hash function. The client generates a new cookie for each connection, and the server can regenerate the cookie by hashing the same inputs.

The server maintains one or two secret values at any time to allow key rotation. Each secret has a state: Generating (newly created, not yet primary), Primary (used for both generation and verification), Retiring (used for verification only), or Secondary (used for fallback verification). Secrets are changed periodically, typically every 600 seconds, and are never stored to disk.
sections.eli5: The cookie is like a sealed letter. The server writes a secret message inside, and only the server knows what is written. When the client brings the sealed letter back, the server opens it and checks that it says what it expects.

sections.title: Extended TCP Headers and Options
sections.content:
The cookie pairs are large (typically 16 bytes each) and do not fit in the standard 40-byte TCP option space alongside other options. Once the cookie exchange succeeds, TCPCT allows TCP header extension. The extended header option carries larger timestamps (64-bit or 128-bit instead of 32-bit).

The extended header also provides space for other large options like the Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) option. This allows TCPCT to simultaneously address spoofing and carry more information during connection establishment.
sections.eli5: The cookie and token are too big to fit in the normal envelope. Once both sides have exchanged them, they can use a bigger envelope for sending more information.

sections.title: Accelerated Open and Close
sections.content:
TCPCT supports optional accelerated open, allowing the client to send data in the SYN packet and the server to send data in the SYN-ACK, reducing round trips for transaction-style applications.

TCPCT also supports accelerated close. Since the server does not retain state after the initial exchange, the connection can be closed quickly with cookies and timestamps protecting against spoofing. The client handles the TIME-WAIT state instead of the server, reducing server overhead.
sections.eli5: Once both sides have proven they are real with cookies, they can send actual work right away without waiting. And when closing, the server can drop the record immediately because it was never really keeping it.
